At the dataset level, \citet{Penedo2024} documented quality filtering strategies for 15T-token web corpora, and \citet{Zhang2026} (concurrent preprint) proposed a unified quality-trustworthiness evaluation taxonomy for synthetic data.
\citet{Gambetta2024} introduced surplexity to quantify diversity loss from synthetic contamination at various mixture fractions, providing an output-level post-hoc analysis.
\citet{Wang2025_scaling} discovered three-phase scaling behavior and tail truncation effects in real-synthetic data mixtures for LLM training.

These methods answer whether synthetic data is \emph{present}; our work addresses how severely it has \emph{degraded} the model.
Detection is inherently post-hoc---applied to static datasets or finished models---while our monitoring operates in real time during training.
Moreover, detection methods do not quantify collapse severity or provide actionable stopping criteria.


\subsection{Positioning of This Work}

Across nearly 50 surveyed papers spanning collapse theory, spectral analysis, training dynamics, and data quality, no prior work simultaneously achieves: (a) online monitoring during training, (b) spectral and entropic training-dynamic signals, (c) per-layer granularity, and (d) validation in the iterative synthetic data setting.
We bridge the gap between collapse theory---which establishes \emph{that} degradation occurs---and practitioner needs for \emph{when} and \emph{how severely} it manifests.
Our signal taxonomy characterizes the operating ranges where each signal family succeeds, saturates, or misleads, providing actionable guidance absent from prior work.
The early warning capability (detecting collapse at 3\% training progress) addresses the absence of training-time stopping criteria identified in our literature survey.

4	\section{Discussion}
5	\label{sec:discussion}
6	
7	\subsection{Practical Three-Tier Monitoring Recommendation}
8	\label{sec:three_tier}
9	
10	No single signal suffices for collapse monitoring across all operating regimes.
11	Our results motivate a three-tier strategy that assigns each signal family to the task where it excels:
12	
13	\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
14	    \item \textbf{Within-generation alarm} $\to$ stable rank.
15	    Stable rank achieves $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.94$ at 10\% training progress ($0.984$ pooled), with $\Delta_\mathrm{SR} = 34.4\%$ at step~50 (3\% of training).
16	    This structural sensitivity---detecting energy dispersal across representation dimensions before output-level metrics respond---provides the earliest actionable warning.
17	
18	    \item \textbf{Cross-generation severity tracking} $\to$ evaluation perplexity.
19	    With a large absolute effect size ($d = 20.82$) and monotonic growth across generations, evaluation perplexity provides an interpretable severity scale that maps directly to language modeling quality on held-out text.
20	
21	    \item \textbf{Severity discrimination} $\to$ spectral entropy.
22	    The largest effect size ($d = 33.48$) and lowest coefficient of variation ($\mathrm{CV} = 0.0015$) across seeds make spectral entropy the most reproducible discriminator between contamination levels.
23	\end{enumerate}
24	
25	\noindent
26	This assignment reflects a core finding: the signal that best detects collapse onset (stable rank, $\mathrm{CV} = 0.022$, seed-sensitive) differs from the one that most reproducibly quantifies its severity (spectral entropy).
27	
28	\subsection{Evaluation Perplexity: Within-Generation Failure Mechanism}
29	\label{sec:ppl_failure}
30	
31	Evaluation perplexity achieves only overall $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.533$---indistinguishable from chance---despite being the primary severity indicator across generations.
32	As discussed in Section~\ref{sec:early_warning_results}, this failure is structural: collapse pressure enters only at the next generation, so evaluation perplexity accumulates degradation through the iterative loop, not within a single run.
33	Train loss ($\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.923$ at completion) is the second-strongest within-generation signal, but its trajectory reveals early-training direction reversal: AUROC starts at $0.24$ at 10\% progress (below chance) because the collapsing model's loss is initially \emph{lower}, recovering only as cumulative degradation raises loss in the second half of training (Section~\ref{sec:early_warning_results}).
34	For practitioners, the implication is that evaluation perplexity is a lagging indicator of collapse, and train loss changes require spectral cross-validation to interpret correctly.
35	
36	\subsection{Partial Recovery at Moderate Contamination}
37	\label{sec:recovery}
38	
39	At $\alpha = 0.5$, some signals show partial recovery across generations: output signals recover approximately 52\% of the clean-to-collapsed gap, while weight-space signals recover approximately 33\%.
40	This pattern is consistent with the data accumulation effects documented by \citet{Gerstgrasser2024}, where mixing real data with synthetic data attenuates collapse.
41	We note this as an observation, not a novel finding.
42	The practical consequence is that monitoring thresholds should be calibrated to the expected contamination level rather than set as binary collapsed/not-collapsed decisions.
43	
44	\subsection{Comparison with Concurrent Monitoring Approaches}
45	\label{sec:sigma_comparison}
46	
47	The signals evaluated here incur near-zero marginal cost: they are computed from quantities already available during standard training, require no clean reference distribution, and provide per-layer granularity.
48	SIGMA~\citep{Gu2026} operates post-hoc on the output embedding Gram matrix and requires a clean reference distribution for comparison.
49	\citet{Kalinowski2026} uses persistent homology, incurring higher computational cost from a different signal family entirely.
50	Neither provides the systematic comparison of signal families, operating range characterization across contamination fractions, or within-generation early warning documented here.
51	These approaches are complementary: SIGMA and topological methods may capture aspects of collapse that spectral covariance signals miss, while our signals offer the advantage of online, reference-free monitoring integrated into the training loop.
52	
53	\subsection{Terminal Spectral Convergence}
54	\label{sec:terminal_convergence}
55	
56	At generation~4, $\alpha = 1.0$, terminal stable rank values are $\mathrm{SR} = 153.87$ (full fine-tuning) versus $155.64$ (QLoRA)---a 1.2\% difference despite markedly different collapse dynamics (onset ratio $15.3\times$ vs $8.7\times$; terminal $\mathrm{PPL}_\text{eval}$ of $326.19$ vs $839.2$).
57	This observation rests on $N = 1$ seed per method and cannot be distinguished from coincidence.
58	If real, it would suggest that iterative synthetic contamination drives representations toward a method-independent attractor in spectral space---a convergence in representational structure despite divergent output-level severity.
59	Multi-seed validation is required before this can be treated as anything more than speculation.
60

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

\subsection{Practical Three-Tier Monitoring Recommendation}
\label{sec:three_tier}

No single signal suffices for collapse monitoring across all operating regimes.
Our results motivate a three-tier strategy that assigns each signal family to the task where it excels:

\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
    \item \textbf{Within-generation alarm} $\to$ stable rank.
    Stable rank achieves $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.94$ at 10\% training progress ($0.984$ pooled), with $\Delta_\mathrm{SR} = 34.4\%$ at step~50 (3\% of training).
    This structural sensitivity---detecting energy dispersal across representation dimensions before output-level metrics respond---provides the earliest actionable warning.

    \item \textbf{Cross-generation severity tracking} $\to$ evaluation perplexity.
    With a large absolute effect size ($d = 20.82$) and monotonic growth across generations, evaluation perplexity provides an interpretable severity scale that maps directly to language modeling quality on held-out text.

    \item \textbf{Severity discrimination} $\to$ spectral entropy.
    The largest effect size ($d = 33.48$) and lowest coefficient of variation ($\mathrm{CV} = 0.0015$) across seeds make spectral entropy the most reproducible discriminator between contamination levels.
\end{enumerate}

\noindent
This assignment reflects a core finding: the signal that best detects collapse onset (stable rank, $\mathrm{CV} = 0.022$, seed-sensitive) differs from the one that most reproducibly quantifies its severity (spectral entropy).

\subsection{Evaluation Perplexity: Within-Generation Failure Mechanism}
\label{sec:ppl_failure}

Evaluation perplexity achieves only overall $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.533$---indistinguishable from chance---despite being the primary severity indicator across generations.
As discussed in Section~\ref{sec:early_warning_results}, this failure is structural: collapse pressure enters only at the next generation, so evaluation perplexity accumulates degradation through the iterative loop, not within a single run.
Train loss ($\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.923$ at completion) is the second-strongest within-generation signal, but its trajectory reveals early-training direction reversal: AUROC starts at $0.24$ at 10\% progress (below chance) because the collapsing model's loss is initially \emph{lower}, recovering only as cumulative degradation raises loss in the second half of training (Section~\ref{sec:early_warning_results}).
For practitioners, the implication is that evaluation perplexity is a lagging indicator of collapse, and train loss changes require spectral cross-validation to interpret correctly.

\subsection{Partial Recovery at Moderate Contamination}
\label{sec:recovery}

At $\alpha = 0.5$, some signals show partial recovery across generations: output signals recover approximately 52\% of the clean-to-collapsed gap, while weight-space signals recover approximately 33\%.
This pattern is consistent with the data accumulation effects documented by \citet{Gerstgrasser2024}, where mixing real data with synthetic data attenuates collapse.
We note this as an observation, not a novel finding.
The practical consequence is that monitoring thresholds should be calibrated to the expected contamination level rather than set as binary collapsed/not-collapsed decisions.

\subsection{Comparison with Concurrent Monitoring Approaches}
\label{sec:sigma_comparison}

The signals evaluated here incur near-zero marginal cost: they are computed from quantities already available during standard training, require no clean reference distribution, and provide per-layer granularity.
SIGMA~\citep{Gu2026} operates post-hoc on the output embedding Gram matrix and requires a clean reference distribution for comparison.
\citet{Kalinowski2026} uses persistent homology, incurring higher computational cost from a different signal family entirely.
Neither provides the systematic comparison of signal families, operating range characterization across contamination fractions, or within-generation early warning documented here.
These approaches are complementary: SIGMA and topological methods may capture aspects of collapse that spectral covariance signals miss, while our signals offer the advantage of online, reference-free monitoring integrated into the training loop.

\subsection{Terminal Spectral Convergence}
\label{sec:terminal_convergence}

At generation~4, $\alpha = 1.0$, terminal stable rank values are $\mathrm{SR} = 153.87$ (full fine-tuning) versus $155.64$ (QLoRA)---a 1.2\% difference despite markedly different collapse dynamics (onset ratio $15.3\times$ vs $8.7\times$; terminal $\mathrm{PPL}_\text{eval}$ of $326.19$ vs $839.2$).
This observation rests on $N = 1$ seed per method and cannot be distinguished from coincidence.
If real, it would suggest that iterative synthetic contamination drives representations toward a method-independent attractor in spectral space---a convergence in representational structure despite divergent output-level severity.
Multi-seed validation is required before this can be treated as anything more than speculation.

% Limitations section — collapse_severity_monitor

Our study has several limitations that bound the scope of our conclusions.

\paragraph{Scale.}
Our primary experiments use Qwen2.5-0.5B and 1.5B models, with only a single-seed spot-check at 3B.
Whether signal--severity relationships and operating ranges transfer to models at scales of practical deployment ($\geq$7B) remains unvalidated.
Stable rank baselines are known to be scale-dependent~\citep{Jha2025}, and threshold calibration may require per-scale adjustment.

\paragraph{Seed count and statistical power.}
Cross-generation effect sizes are computed from $N = 3$ seeds (C2 configuration, interim 3 of 5 planned seeds); within-generation AUROC results use $N = 1$ seed at 0.5B (C1).
The full fine-tuning comparison (C4) uses $N = 1$ seed.
These sample sizes are insufficient for rank-based tests (minimum $p = 0.25$ for Wilcoxon with $N = 3$), and we rely on bootstrap confidence intervals.
Stable rank's coefficient of variation ($\mathrm{CV} = 0.022$) is an order of magnitude larger than spectral entropy's ($0.0015$), and its effect size dropped from $d = 61.7$ to $d = 9.43$ when a third seed was added---underscoring that our ranking of signals by sensitivity may shift with more seeds.

\paragraph{Domain coverage.}
We evaluate on WikiText-2 and PubMed abstracts.
Whether our signal taxonomy generalizes to code, dialogue, multilingual text, or instruction-following data is unknown.

\paragraph{Collapse source.}
Our iterative retraining protocol simulates a specific collapse mechanism---self-consuming loops with controlled contamination fractions.
Real-world collapse may involve mixed provenance (multiple model generations), distribution shift between generations, or partial synthetic contamination at unknown fractions.
Signal behavior under these conditions may differ from our controlled setting.

\paragraph{Fine-tuning methods.}
We compare QLoRA and full fine-tuning.
Other parameter-efficient methods (LoRA without quantization, adapters, prefix tuning) may interact differently with spectral signals due to different parameterization constraints.

\paragraph{Causal claims.}
We establish correlations between signals and collapse severity, not causal mechanisms.
The spectral entropy increase under collapse reflects a change in representation structure, but we do not prove that this change causes (rather than accompanies) output degradation.

276	\subsection{Bootstrap Confidence Intervals}
277	\label{app:bootstrap}
278	
279	We employ clustered bootstrap resampling to compute 95\% confidence intervals for all reported correlations and effect sizes.
280	The cluster unit is the (fraction, seed) pair, yielding $6 \times 5 = 30$ independent clusters in the full experimental design.
281	Within each bootstrap iteration ($B = 10{,}000$ resamples), we resample clusters with replacement and recompute the statistic of interest.
282	This accounts for the within-run dependence across generations: generation $g+1$ trains on data produced by the model from generation $g$, so observations within a (fraction, seed) run are causally linked.
283	
284	Pooling individual generation observations as independent samples would inflate the effective sample size from 30 to 150, producing artificially narrow intervals.
285	Our clustered approach yields conservative but honest intervals that reflect the true experimental degrees of freedom.

\subsection{Synthetic Data Generation}
\label{app:data_gen}
%% Source: mvp_frac50_100 — generation config

At each generation $g$, we sample synthetic text from the fine-tuned model $\tilde{M}_g$ using the following procedure:

\begin{itemize}[nosep]
    \item \textbf{Prompting:} The first 32 tokens of each randomly subsampled real-text chunk serve as the prompt.
    \item \textbf{Decoding:} Nucleus sampling with temperature $\tau = 1.0$ and top-$p = 0.95$.
    \item \textbf{Max new tokens:} 480 (total sequence length $\leq 512$).
    \item \textbf{Subsample size:} 1{,}500 chunks per generation (from $|\mathcal{D}_\text{real}| = 4{,}916$).
\end{itemize}

\noindent
The fixed prompt length ensures that synthetic and real chunks share distributional overlap at the beginning, isolating divergence to model-generated continuations.

\subsection{Evaluation Details}
\label{app:eval_details}
%% Source: mvp_frac50_100 — evaluation config

\paragraph{HellaSwag evaluation.}
We evaluate HellaSwag~\citep{zellers2019hellaswag} using 1{,}000 randomly sampled instances in 4-choice format.
For each instance, the model scores each candidate continuation by computing its per-token log-likelihood conditioned on the context, selecting the highest-scoring option.
Evaluation is performed at the end of each generation (not at intermediate checkpoints) due to computational cost.

\paragraph{Perplexity and token entropy.}
Both are computed on the held-out WikiText-2 validation set using 100 validation chunks.
Perplexity uses the standard cross-entropy formulation (Eq.~\ref{eq:perplexity}); token entropy averages per-position next-token entropy (Eq.~\ref{eq:token_entropy}) over all positions in the validation set.

\paragraph{Spectral signals.}
Stable rank and spectral entropy are computed from the last-layer hidden-state covariance matrix using 64 validation chunks.
We retain the top-5 singular values for trajectory logging; the full eigenspectrum is used for stable rank and spectral entropy computation.

\section{Statistical Analysis}
\label{app:stats}

\subsection{Bootstrap Confidence Intervals}
\label{app:bootstrap}

We employ clustered bootstrap resampling to compute 95\% confidence intervals for all reported correlations and effect sizes.
The cluster unit is the (fraction, seed) pair, yielding $6 \times 5 = 30$ independent clusters in the full experimental design.
Within each bootstrap iteration ($B = 10{,}000$ resamples), we resample clusters with replacement and recompute the statistic of interest.
This accounts for the within-run dependence across generations: generation $g+1$ trains on data produced by the model from generation $g$, so observations within a (fraction, seed) run are causally linked.

Pooling individual generation observations as independent samples would inflate the effective sample size from 30 to 150, producing artificially narrow intervals.
Our clustered approach yields conservative but honest intervals that reflect the true experimental degrees of freedom.

## Abstract

\begin{abstract}
Iterative training on model-generated data causes model collapse---progressive loss of distribution tails, contraction of output diversity, and degradation of acquired knowledge---yet the metrics practitioners most commonly watch during training fail to detect it.
We systematically evaluate four families of training-time signals---spectral (stable rank, spectral entropy), output (train loss, evaluation perplexity, token entropy), gradient (L2 norm), and downstream (HellaSwag accuracy)---as collapse severity monitors across five experimental configurations spanning model scales (0.5B--3B), fine-tuning methods (QLoRA, full fine-tuning), contamination fractions ($\alpha \in \{0, 0.1, \ldots, 1.0\}$), and text domains (WikiText-2, PubMed).
We find that different signal families have complementary operating ranges.
Spectral entropy achieves the largest cross-generation effect size (Cohen's $d = 33.48$, $\mathrm{CV} = 0.0015$ across seeds), while stable rank provides the strongest within-generation early warning ($\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.94$ at 10\% training progress, $0.984$ pooled, 34.4\% deviation at 3\% of training).
Held-out evaluation perplexity provides no within-generation early warning (pooled $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.533$, indistinguishable from random), while train loss is an effective but interpretively ambiguous detector (pooled $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.923$): its decrease reflects successful fitting of corrupted data, not improved model quality.
The same signal can be informative under one training method and misleading under another: gradient norm is non-monotonic under QLoRA but monotonic under full fine-tuning.
These findings yield a three-tier monitoring strategy---stable rank for within-generation alarms, evaluation perplexity for cross-generation tracking, spectral entropy for severity discrimination---and a signal taxonomy characterizing where each family succeeds, saturates, or misleads.
\end{abstract}

---

## Section 1: Introduction

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

As LLM-generated text pervades web-scraped training corpora, practitioners increasingly fine-tune models on data shaped by prior model generations.
This recursive dynamic creates self-consuming loops that cause \emph{model collapse}---progressive loss of distribution tails, contraction of output diversity, and degradation of acquired knowledge~\citep{Shumailov2024,Alemohammad2024}.
The problem compounds: even trace synthetic contamination induces collapse at sufficient depth~\citep{Dohmatob2025}, with errors accumulating across iterations at accelerating rates~\citep{Dohmatob2024_tails,Fu2024_icml}.
Yet the metric practitioners most commonly rely on for quality assessment---held-out evaluation perplexity---fails to detect this degradation within a run, achieving pooled $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.533$ for within-generation collapse detection (indistinguishable from random chance).
Train loss does change under collapse (pooled $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.923$), but its decrease is interpretively ambiguous: the model fits lower-entropy synthetic data more easily, which looks like healthy convergence.
A practitioner watching only perplexity or interpreting train loss at face value would have no reliable warning that collapse is underway.

Existing work addresses model collapse from two directions.
On the theoretical side, \citet{Shumailov2024} established the phenomenon, \citet{Dohmatob2025} proved that any nonzero synthetic fraction eventually induces strong collapse, and \citet{Dohmatob2024_tails} showed that collapse alters neural scaling laws.
On the mitigation side, data accumulation~\citep{Gerstgrasser2024}, loss modification~\citep{Zibakhsh2025}, and verification-based filtering~\citep{Feng2025} each reduce collapse pressure under specific conditions.
Missing from this landscape is a systematic analysis of which \emph{training-time signals} best track collapse severity, when they provide early warning, and where they saturate or actively mislead.
\citet{Schaeffer2025} highlight that even the definition of collapse varies across studies, further motivating signal-level analysis grounded in controlled experiments.
The two closest concurrent works---SIGMA~\citep{Gu2026}, which monitors output embedding spectra, and the topological index of \citet{Kalinowski2026}---each address part of this gap but carry limitations: SIGMA requires a clean reference distribution and operates post-hoc; topological monitoring incurs higher computational cost.
Neither provides a cross-family comparison of signal operating ranges or quantitative within-generation early warning thresholds.

We conduct a systematic empirical study of training-time signals as collapse severity monitors.
We evaluate four signal families---spectral (stable rank, spectral entropy), output (train loss, evaluation perplexity, token entropy), gradient (L2 norm), and downstream (HellaSwag accuracy)---across five experimental configurations spanning model scales (0.5B to 3B), fine-tuning methods (QLoRA and full fine-tuning), contamination fractions ($\alpha \in \{0, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0\}$), and text domains (WikiText-2, PubMed).
Our central finding is that different signal families have complementary operating ranges, and the same signal's utility can flip from informative to misleading depending on the training method.

Our contributions:

\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Signal--severity correlation.}
    Spectral and output signals track collapse across contamination levels.
    Spectral entropy achieves the largest effect size (Cohen's $d = 33.48$, coefficient of variation $\mathrm{CV} = 0.0015$ across seeds), followed by evaluation perplexity ($d = 20.82$) and stable rank ($d = 9.43$, $\mathrm{CV} = 0.022$).
    Validated across QLoRA and full fine-tuning, six of seven monitored signals maintain consistent direction of change regardless of training method.
    The exception---gradient norm, which is non-monotonic under QLoRA but monotonic under full fine-tuning---demonstrates that method-dependence is a first-order concern for monitoring pipeline design.

    \item \textbf{Within-generation early warning and negative results.}
    Stable rank achieves $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.94$ at 10\% training progress ($0.984$ pooled) for binary collapse detection, with 34.4\% deviation from baseline at 3\% of training.
    Train loss provides the second-strongest within-generation signal (pooled $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.923$), though its decrease reflects successful fitting of corrupted data rather than improved model quality.
    Held-out evaluation perplexity achieves pooled $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.533$ for within-generation detection---the most commonly relied-upon quality metric fails at the most actionable task---and token entropy achieves pooled $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.478$, providing no reliable discrimination despite a large initial deviation.
    Evaluation perplexity's failure has a structural explanation: it accumulates degradation through the iterative contamination loop, not within a single generation's training.

    \item \textbf{Signal taxonomy with method-dependent operating ranges.}
    Signal informativeness depends on the fine-tuning method and model scale.
    Gradient norm is non-monotonic under QLoRA but monotonic under full fine-tuning.
    HellaSwag accuracy is insensitive at 0.5B scale (relative change ${<}3\%$, $N{=}1$).
    Distinct-1 is non-monotonic, reversing direction between moderate and full contamination.
    Full fine-tuning produces sharper collapse onset ($15.3\times$ evaluation perplexity ratio at generation~1) than QLoRA ($8.7\times$) but lower terminal severity.
    These findings motivate a three-tier recommendation: stable rank for within-generation alarms, evaluation perplexity for cross-generation tracking, and spectral entropy for severity discrimination.
\end{enumerate}

Section~\ref{sec:related_work} surveys collapse theory, spectral analysis of neural networks, and concurrent monitoring approaches.
Section~\ref{sec:method} details our iterative contamination protocol, signal definitions, and evaluation framework.
Section~\ref{sec:results} presents signal--severity correlations, within-generation early warning analysis, and the method-dependent signal taxonomy.
Section~\ref{sec:discussion} discusses practical monitoring recommendations and limitations.
Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} concludes.

---

## Section 2: Related Work

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related_work}

\subsection{Model Collapse in Iterative Training}

The phenomenon of model collapse---progressive degradation when models are iteratively trained on their own outputs---has been established across multiple generative families.
\citet{Shumailov2024} provided the first systematic demonstration that iterative training on synthetic data causes distribution tails to vanish, leading to irreversible quality loss in LLMs, VAEs, and GMMs.
\citet{Alemohammad2024} formalized three self-consuming loop variants (fully synthetic, synthetic augmentation, and fresh data mixing), proving that without fresh real data, either precision or recall must degrade.
Theoretical analyses have since strengthened these findings: \citet{Dohmatob2025} proved via operator-valued free probability theory that even a $1/1000$ synthetic data fraction induces collapse and that larger models amplify the effect, while \citet{Dohmatob2024_tails} showed collapse alters scaling laws and induces systematic skill un-learning.
Further theoretical work has characterized error compounding across iterations~\citep{Fu2024_icml}, established safety thresholds for synthetic data fractions under statistical models~\citep{Seddik2024}, and revealed a generalization-to-memorization transition driven by data entropy~\citep{Shi2025_neurips}.
\citet{Schaeffer2025} catalogued eight distinct collapse definitions across three families, highlighting the need for precise operationalization.

Several lines of work study \emph{prevention} rather than detection.
\citet{Gerstgrasser2024} showed that data accumulation (rather than replacement) avoids collapse; \citet{Kazdan2024} systematically compared replacement, accumulation, and fixed-compute regimes; and verification-based approaches filter synthetic data to maintain quality~\citep{Feng2025,Yi2025}.
\citet{Gillman2024} demonstrated that correction functions can exponentially stabilize self-consuming loops, while \citet{Zibakhsh2025} proposed a truncated cross-entropy loss that increases tolerance to synthetic contamination by $2.3\times$.
\citet{Bakshi2026} (concurrent preprint) proved that even diminishing real data weights can prevent collapse in the long run.

These works collectively establish \emph{that} collapse occurs and \emph{how} to mitigate it, but they rely on post-hoc evaluation (test loss, distribution divergence) or require prior knowledge of contamination levels.
No prior work provides a real-time, training-time monitoring framework that tracks collapse severity as it develops.


\subsection{Training Dynamics as Diagnostic Signals}

\paragraph{Spectral analysis of neural networks.}
Spectral properties of weight matrices have emerged as powerful diagnostics for model quality and training health.
\citet{Martin2021} demonstrated that stable rank, spectral norm, and power-law exponents of weight spectra predict model quality without test data, establishing a random matrix theory (RMT) framework for neural network analysis.
\citet{Sanyal2020} proved a direct link between stable rank and generalization gap, showing that stable rank normalization improves generalization by up to 11.3\%.
More recently, \citet{Xu2026} (concurrent preprint) found stable rank to be the dominant predictor of LLM compression degradation (Pearson $r=0.890$) with informative per-layer variation between attention and MLP modules.
On the theoretical side, \citet{Pennington2017} extended RMT to nonlinear settings, deriving asymptotic spectral distributions through network layers.
\citet{Yunis2024} used spectral dynamics of weights to distinguish memorizing from generalizing networks, while \citet{AlphaPruning2024} validated per-layer spectral analysis for LLM quality assessment via alpha-exponent-guided pruning.

Spectral scaling across model sizes has received increasing attention.
\citet{Jha2025} discovered that FFN soft rank scales near-linearly with width while hard rank grows sub-linearly, implying that stable rank baselines are scale-dependent.
\citet{Staats2024} showed via RMT analysis across BERT, Pythia-410M, and Llama-8B that small singular values carry significant information, cautioning against truncated spectral analyses.
\citet{Liu2026_lifecycle} (concurrent preprint) documented the full spectral lifecycle of transformer training across three scales (30M--285M), revealing that stable rank compression propagates as a traveling wave from shallow to deep layers with Q/K and V/O asymmetries.

\paragraph{Training dynamics for data and training quality.}
Beyond weight spectra, training-time signals have been used to diagnose data quality and training health.
\citet{Li2025_gradient} showed that layer-wise gradient SVD effective rank and nuclear norm unify multiple data quality metrics, with higher effective rank indicating higher data quality.
\citet{Elgaar2026} (concurrent preprint) used gradient noise scale and singular entropy of the output head as LLM training diagnostics in curriculum learning.
\citet{Chen2024_dse} proposed diffusion spectral entropy (DSE) to track training dynamics, observing that information-theoretic measures stagnate at overfitting onset.
\citet{Qiu2025} introduced spectral alignment between layer inputs and weight principal singular vectors as an early predictor of loss explosion, detecting pathologies before gradient norms diverge.
\citet{Kalra2026} (concurrent preprint) proposed critical sharpness as a lightweight loss landscape curvature measure validated at 7B scale.

\paragraph{Closest competitors.}
Two concurrent works most directly relate to ours.
\textbf{SIGMA}~\citep{Gu2026} (concurrent preprint) analyzes the Gram matrix spectrum of output embeddings to quantify collapse, deriving spectral contraction bounds.
However, SIGMA operates as a post-hoc, black-box diagnostic: it requires a clean reference distribution, does not perform per-layer analysis, does not track within-generation training dynamics, and has not been validated in the iterative synthetic data setting.
\textbf{Kalinowski}~\citep{Kalinowski2026} (concurrent preprint) proposes an online topological monitor based on persistent homology with sparse incremental updates.
While this shares our goal of real-time monitoring, it uses a fundamentally different signal family (topological rather than spectral/entropic), incurs higher computational cost, and has not been evaluated on iterative synthetic data collapse.
Table~\ref{tab:competitor_comparison} summarizes the key differences.

Neither approach provides a systematic comparison of multiple signal families, documents where signals saturate or mislead, or establishes quantitative early warning thresholds for iterative collapse.


\subsection{Data Quality and Contamination Detection}

A parallel line of work addresses detection of synthetic data in training corpora.
Watermarking approaches embed identifiable patterns in generated text: \citet{Kirchenbauer2023} introduced green/red token list watermarking with statistical detection, while \citet{Dathathri2024} scaled watermarking to production (SynthID-Text, validated on ${\sim}$20M Gemini responses) and \citet{Sander2024} showed that watermark residuals can detect whether a model was trained on watermarked synthetic data.
Statistical detection methods identify machine-generated text without explicit watermarks: \citet{Mitchell2023} exploited log-probability curvature for zero-shot detection (DetectGPT), and \citet{Shi2024_mink} proposed Min-K\% Prob for membership inference in pretraining data.
At the dataset level, \citet{Penedo2024} documented quality filtering strategies for 15T-token web corpora, and \citet{Zhang2026} (concurrent preprint) proposed a unified quality-trustworthiness evaluation taxonomy for synthetic data.
\citet{Gambetta2024} introduced surplexity to quantify diversity loss from synthetic contamination at various mixture fractions, providing an output-level post-hoc analysis.
\citet{Wang2025_scaling} discovered three-phase scaling behavior and tail truncation effects in real-synthetic data mixtures for LLM training.

These methods answer whether synthetic data is \emph{present}; our work addresses how severely it has \emph{degraded} the model.
Detection is inherently post-hoc---applied to static datasets or finished models---while our monitoring operates in real time during training.
Moreover, detection methods do not quantify collapse severity or provide actionable stopping criteria.


\subsection{Positioning of This Work}

Across nearly 50 surveyed papers spanning collapse theory, spectral analysis, training dynamics, and data quality, no prior work simultaneously achieves: (a) online monitoring during training, (b) spectral and entropic training-dynamic signals, (c) per-layer granularity, and (d) validation in the iterative synthetic data setting.
We bridge the gap between collapse theory---which establishes \emph{that} degradation occurs---and practitioner needs for \emph{when} and \emph{how severely} it manifests.
Our signal taxonomy characterizes the operating ranges where each signal family succeeds, saturates, or misleads, providing actionable guidance absent from prior work.
The early warning capability (detecting collapse at 3\% training progress) addresses the absence of training-time stopping criteria identified in our literature survey.

---

## Section 3: Methodology

\section{Methodology}
\label{sec:method}

We design a controlled framework to evaluate how training-time signals track model collapse severity under iterative synthetic data contamination.
Our protocol varies contamination level and generational depth while monitoring four families of signals across five experimental configurations.

\subsection{Iterative Training Protocol}
\label{sec:protocol}

We simulate iterative model collapse through a multi-generation fine-tuning loop.
Let $M_0$ denote a pretrained base model and $\mathcal{D}_\text{real}$ a corpus of real text.
At each generation $g \in \{0, 1, \ldots, G{-}1\}$ (with $G=5$), we execute three steps:

\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Fine-tune.} Initialize from $M_0$ and fine-tune on the current training corpus $\mathcal{D}_g$, yielding model $\tilde{M}_g$. During training, we collect monitoring signals every 50 optimizer steps via a callback on a held-out validation set (Section~\ref{sec:signals}).
    \item \textbf{Generate.} Sample synthetic text $\mathcal{S}_g$ from $\tilde{M}_g$ by prompting with the first 32 tokens of randomly subsampled chunks from $\mathcal{D}_\text{real}$ and generating up to 480 new tokens with nucleus sampling ($p=0.95$, temperature $\tau=1.0$). We subsample 1{,}500 chunks for generation.
    \item \textbf{Mix.} Construct the next-generation corpus by replacing fraction $\alpha$ of real chunks with synthetic chunks:
    \begin{equation}
        \mathcal{D}_{g+1} = (1 - \alpha)\,\mathcal{D}_\text{real} \cup \alpha\,\mathcal{S}_g.
        \label{eq:mixing}
    \end{equation}
\end{enumerate}

\noindent
Each generation initializes from the \emph{same} pretrained weights $M_0$, isolating the effect of data contamination from cumulative weight drift.
Collapse pressure enters solely through the training corpus: at generation $g$, the synthetic component was produced by a model trained on data that itself contained synthetic text from generation $g{-}1$.

All fine-tuning runs use AdamW with learning rate $2 \times 10^{-4}$, weight decay $0.01$, linear warmup over $5\%$ of steps, and gradient clipping at $\|\cdot\|_2 \leq 1.0$.
We train for 5 epochs with effective batch size 16 (per-device batch 4, gradient accumulation 4) in \texttt{bf16} mixed precision.
QLoRA configurations~\citep{dettmers2023qlora} use rank $r=16$, scaling factor $\alpha_\text{LoRA}=32$, dropout $0.05$, with adapters on all linear projections (\texttt{q\_proj}, \texttt{k\_proj}, \texttt{v\_proj}, \texttt{o\_proj}, \texttt{up\_proj}, \texttt{down\_proj}, \texttt{gate\_proj}); the base model is quantized to 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4) with double quantization.
Full fine-tuning (C4; Table~\ref{tab:configs}) uses identical hyperparameters with all parameters trainable and no quantization.

\subsection{Contamination Fractions}
\label{sec:fractions}

We test six contamination levels: $\alpha \in \{0, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0\}$.
The $\alpha=0$ condition serves as a clean baseline, controlling for training noise and natural run-to-run variance in the absence of synthetic contamination.
The $\alpha=1.0$ condition replaces the entire training set with synthetic data, applying maximum collapse pressure.
Intermediate fractions trace the dose--response relationship between contamination level and signal behavior.

\subsection{Monitoring Signals}
\label{sec:signals}

We monitor four families of training-time signals (seven signals total), collected every 50 optimizer steps.
Spectral signals and evaluation perplexity are computed on a held-out validation set in evaluation mode; train loss is logged from the training set by the Trainer.

\paragraph{Spectral signals.}
Given $n$ validation sequences, we collect last-layer hidden states into a matrix $\mathbf{H} \in \mathbb{R}^{T \times d}$ ($T$ total tokens, $d$ hidden dimension), center by subtracting the column mean, and compute the sample covariance $\mathbf{C} = \frac{1}{T-1}\mathbf{H}^\top\mathbf{H}$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_1 \geq \cdots \geq \lambda_d \geq 0$.

\emph{Stable rank} measures the effective dimensionality of the representation:
\begin{equation}
    \mathrm{SR}(\mathbf{C}) = \frac{\left(\sum_{i=1}^{d} \lambda_i\right)^2}{\sum_{i=1}^{d} \lambda_i^2}.
    \label{eq:stable_rank}
\end{equation}
Under model collapse, $\mathrm{SR}$ \emph{increases}: the Frobenius norm $\|\mathbf{H}\|_F^2$ grows faster than the leading eigenvalue $\lambda_1$, dispersing energy across more dimensions rather than concentrating it.

\emph{Spectral entropy} provides a complementary measure of spectral concentration:
\begin{equation}
    \mathrm{SE}(\mathbf{C}) = \frac{-\sum_{i=1}^{d} p_i \log p_i}{\log d}, \quad p_i = \frac{\lambda_i}{\sum_{j=1}^{d} \lambda_j}.
    \label{eq:spectral_entropy}
\end{equation}
$\mathrm{SE} \in [0,1]$, with $\mathrm{SE}=1$ for a uniform spectrum and $\mathrm{SE} \to 0$ for concentration on few components.
We use $n=64$ validation chunks for SVD computation.

\paragraph{Output signals.}
We monitor three output-level signals computed on different data splits.

\emph{Train loss} $\mathcal{L}_\text{train}$ is the per-batch cross-entropy on the current training corpus, logged every 50 optimizer steps by the HuggingFace Trainer.
Because contaminated data has lower entropy than real text, train loss \emph{decreases} under collapse---the model fits synthetic output easily.
This makes train loss an effective within-generation detector of data distribution change, though a decrease in train loss does not imply improved model quality.

\emph{Evaluation perplexity} is computed on a held-out clean validation set:
\begin{equation}
    \mathrm{PPL}_\text{eval} = \exp\!\left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{|\mathcal{V}|} \ell(\mathbf{x}_i)\right),
    \label{eq:perplexity}
\end{equation}
where $\ell(\mathbf{x}_i)$ is the cross-entropy loss on validation sequence $\mathbf{x}_i$ and $N$ is the total token count.
Evaluation perplexity tracks degradation in language modeling quality on real text across generations, but its within-generation utility is limited (Section~\ref{sec:early_warning_results}).
Note that training perplexity $\mathrm{PPL}_\text{train} = \exp(\mathcal{L}_\text{train})$ is a monotone transform of train loss; we report train loss directly since it is the quantity logged during training.

\emph{Token entropy} measures the mean per-position entropy of the next-token distribution:
\begin{equation}
    \mathrm{TE}(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{L-1}\sum_{t=1}^{L-1} H\!\left(P_\theta(\cdot \mid x_{\leq t})\right), \quad H(P) = -\sum_v P(v) \log P(v),
    \label{eq:token_entropy}
\end{equation}
averaged over 100 validation chunks.
Decreasing token entropy indicates the model is becoming more peaked in its predictions, a hallmark of mode collapse in generation.

\paragraph{Gradient signal.}
We log the L2 gradient norm $\|\nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}\|_2$ before each optimizer step.
Gradient norm is a zero-cost byproduct of standard training.
Under QLoRA, gradient norm exhibits non-monotonic behavior with respect to contamination fraction: gradients flow only through low-rank adapter matrices~\citep{hu2022lora}, confining the landscape to a rank-$r$ subspace, and NF4 quantization of frozen base weights introduces discretization noise that propagates through the backward pass~\citep{dettmers2023qlora}.

\paragraph{Downstream signal.}
We evaluate HellaSwag~\citep{zellers2019hellaswag} accuracy (4-choice commonsense reasoning, 1{,}000 samples) at the end of each generation as a downstream task probe.

\subsection{Experimental Configurations}
\label{sec:configs}

Table~\ref{tab:configs} summarizes our five experimental configurations.
C1 provides initial signal discovery on the smallest model.
C2 is the primary analysis configuration, with five independent seeds providing statistical power for bootstrap confidence intervals and effect size estimation.
C3 tests cross-domain generalization on biomedical text.
C4 isolates method-dependence by comparing full fine-tuning against QLoRA under matched conditions.
C5 provides a scale spot-check at 3B parameters.

(Table 1: Experimental configurations omitted for brevity — see paper)

WikiText-2~\citep{merity2017pointer} is tokenized and chunked into 512-token sequences (4{,}916 training chunks).
PubMed abstracts~\citep{pubmed2024} (C3) undergo identical preprocessing.

\subsection{Evaluation Framework}
\label{sec:evaluation}

\paragraph{Cross-generation severity.}
For each signal $s$ and generation $g$, we compute the Spearman rank correlation $\rho_g^{(s)}$ between contamination fraction $\alpha$ and the end-of-generation signal value across all tested fractions, with 95\% bootstrap confidence intervals.
We report Cohen's $d$ effect sizes between the clean baseline and each contamination level as the primary evidence for signal sensitivity, since rank correlations alone do not convey the magnitude of signal separation.

\paragraph{Within-generation detection.}
We compute the area under the ROC curve (AUROC) for binary collapse detection at each signal checkpoint (every 50 steps), using \emph{clustered bootstrap} resampling.
The cluster unit is fraction$\times$seed rather than individual generation observations.
This is necessary because successive generations within a run are causally dependent---generation $g{+}1$ trains on data produced by the model from generation $g$---so pooling individual observations would inflate the effective sample size and produce artificially narrow confidence intervals.

We also compute the relative deviation at each checkpoint:
\begin{equation}
    \Delta_s(t, \alpha) = \frac{|s_\alpha(t) - s_0(t)|}{|s_0(t)|} \times 100\%,
    \label{eq:deviation}
\end{equation}
where $s_\alpha(t)$ and $s_0(t)$ are signal values at step $t$ for fraction $\alpha$ and the clean baseline.
A signal provides early warning if $\Delta_s(t, \alpha) > 5\%$ within the first 10\% of training steps.

\paragraph{Method-dependence.}
We compare signal trajectories between QLoRA (C1) and full fine-tuning (C4) under matched model size, dataset, and contamination fractions.
Paired differences in end-of-generation signal values quantify whether collapse signatures depend on the fine-tuning method or reflect properties of the data contamination itself.

---

## Section 4: Results

\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}

We organize results around three claims.
Section~\ref{sec:correlation} establishes that spectral and output signals track collapse severity across configurations.
Section~\ref{sec:early_warning_results} shows that certain signals detect collapse within a single training run before evaluation perplexity diverges.
Section~\ref{sec:taxonomy} reveals that signal informativeness depends on the fine-tuning method, motivating a taxonomy of method-dependent operating ranges.

\subsection{Signal--Severity Correlation}
\label{sec:correlation}

We quantify signal sensitivity using Cohen's $d$ between the clean baseline ($\alpha = 0$) and full contamination ($\alpha = 1.0$) at generation~4, computed across three seeds from the C2 configuration (Qwen2.5-1.5B, WikiText-2; interim 3 of 5 planned seeds; Table~\ref{tab:configs}).
Effect sizes, rather than rank correlations, serve as the primary evidence because they convey the magnitude of signal separation, not just its ordering.

\paragraph{Effect sizes.}
Spectral entropy achieves the largest and most reproducible effect size ($d = 33.48$, coefficient of variation across seeds $\mathrm{CV} = 0.0015$), followed by evaluation perplexity ($d = 20.82$), distinct-1 ($d = 14.60$, 1.5B, effective $N=2$ seeds; this large endpoint separation coexists with non-monotonic intermediate behavior at 0.5B, Section~\ref{sec:taxonomy}), and stable rank ($d = 9.43$, $\mathrm{CV} = 0.022$).
Distinct-2 ($d = 7.59$) and distinct-3 ($d = -7.08$; negative because collapse increases trigram repetition) provide moderate separation.
Token entropy, self-BLEU, gradient norm, and HellaSwag accuracy yield small effect sizes ($d < 5$), placing them in a second tier for cross-generation severity discrimination (Figure~\ref{fig:severity_curves}).

Stable rank warrants a cautionary note on seed sensitivity.
With two seeds, $d = 61.7$; adding a third seed reduced this to $d = 9.43$---a rank change from 1st to 4th among monitored signals.
Its $\mathrm{CV}$ of 0.022 is an order of magnitude larger than spectral entropy's 0.0015.
We treat stable rank as informative but seed-sensitive at this sample size; $N = 3$ seeds are insufficient for a Wilcoxon test (minimum $p = 0.25$), and we rely on bootstrap confidence intervals for inference.

\paragraph{Cross-method consistency.}
Six of seven monitored signals maintain consistent direction of change under both QLoRA and full fine-tuning (Figure~\ref{fig:signal_heatmap}): spectral entropy, stable rank, evaluation perplexity, token entropy, distinct-1, and self-BLEU all move in the same direction as contamination increases, regardless of training method.
The exception is gradient norm, which exhibits non-monotonic behavior under QLoRA but monotonic decrease under full fine-tuning (Section~\ref{sec:taxonomy}).

\paragraph{Supporting rank correlations.}
Spearman correlations provide directional confirmation: spectral entropy maintains high $|\rho|$ across generations.
However, $|\rho| = 1.0$ for stable rank across contamination fractions is trivially achieved with few contamination levels and should not be interpreted as strong evidence of monotonicity.
We therefore use Cohen's $d$ as the primary sensitivity measure throughout.


\subsection{Within-Generation Early Warning}
\label{sec:early_warning_results}

Cross-generation tracking (Section~\ref{sec:correlation}) requires completing multiple generations to assess severity.
A more actionable capability is detecting collapse \emph{within} a single training run, enabling early stopping before degradation accumulates.
We evaluate this using the relative deviation $\Delta_s$ (Eq.~\ref{eq:deviation}) and AUROC for binary collapse detection at each checkpoint.

\paragraph{Stable rank as early alarm.}
Stable rank achieves $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.94$ at 10\% training progress for distinguishing $\alpha = 1.0$ from $\alpha = 0$, reaching $0.984$ over the full run (Figure~\ref{fig:roc_curves}; Table~\ref{tab:within_gen_roc}).
At step~50 (3\% of training), $\Delta_\mathrm{SR} = 34.4\%$---far exceeding the 5\% detection threshold defined in Section~\ref{sec:evaluation}.
Stable rank's within-generation sensitivity reflects the structural nature of spectral signals: contamination alters the covariance eigenspectrum before output-level metrics respond, because energy dispersal across representation dimensions (Eq.~\ref{eq:stable_rank}) is detectable even when the model's token-level predictions have not yet degraded.

\paragraph{Spectral and token entropy.}
Token entropy deviates 24.5\% at step~50 but achieves only $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.478$ (pooled)---near random chance, indicating that despite its large initial deviation, token entropy provides no reliable within-generation discrimination.
Spectral entropy achieves pooled $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.773$, providing moderate within-generation discrimination but still substantially below stable rank's pooled $0.984$.

\paragraph{Train loss: effective but interpretively ambiguous.}
Train loss achieves $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.923$ at training completion, the second-strongest within-generation signal after stable rank.
However, its AUROC trajectory reveals early-training direction reversal (Figure~\ref{fig:roc_curves}b): $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.24$ at 10\% progress, rising to $0.48$ at 20\%, $0.85$ at 50\%, and $0.923$ at completion.
The low early AUROC (${<}\,0.5$) indicates that the collapsing run's training loss is initially \emph{lower} than the clean baseline---the model fits the lower-entropy synthetic distribution more easily, a direct manifestation of the collapse mechanism.
As training progresses, cumulative degradation raises loss in the collapsed run, gradually restoring discriminability.
Train loss is therefore unreliable as an early collapse alarm (AUROC below chance for the first ${\sim}20\%$ of training), but effective at completion.
Practitioners should cross-validate with spectral indicators such as stable rank, which achieves $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.94$ from 10\% progress onward.

\paragraph{Evaluation perplexity: no within-generation signal.}
Held-out evaluation perplexity achieves only $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.533$ across the full run---indistinguishable from random.
This failure has a structural explanation: within a single generation, the model trains on a fixed corpus $\mathcal{D}_g$ and has not yet produced the synthetic data that will contaminate $\mathcal{D}_{g+1}$ (Eq.~\ref{eq:mixing}).
Evaluation perplexity accumulates degradation \emph{across} generations through the iterative contamination loop, not within a single run.
Consequently, it does not diverge from baseline within one generation, even when collapse is underway.

Spectral signals, by contrast, detect structural change---the dispersal of representational energy across dimensions---independent of whether the model's held-out predictions have degraded.
This yields a three-level hierarchy of within-generation detection capability (all pooled AUROC): stable rank ($0.984$) detects changes in weight-space structure, train loss ($0.923$) detects changes in training data distribution, and held-out evaluation perplexity ($0.533$) measures generalization quality---which does not diverge within a single generation.
The weakest link in within-generation monitoring is precisely the metric practitioners most commonly check at evaluation checkpoints.


\subsection{Signal Taxonomy: Method-Dependent Operating Ranges}
\label{sec:taxonomy}

The cross-method comparison (C1 vs C4; Table~\ref{tab:configs}) reveals that the same signal can be informative under one training method and misleading under another.

\paragraph{Gradient norm: method-dependent.}
Under QLoRA, gradient norm changes non-monotonically with contamination: $+5.9\%$ at $\alpha = 0.5$ relative to baseline, then $-30.8\%$ at $\alpha = 1.0$.
Under full fine-tuning, gradient norm decreases monotonically ($-58.3\%$ at $\alpha = 1.0$), consistent with the model converging more easily to lower-entropy synthetic data.
The QLoRA non-monotonicity likely arises from the interaction between contaminated gradients and the rank-$r$ adapter subspace~\citep{hu2022lora}: at moderate contamination, gradients from mixed real/synthetic data create conflicting update directions within the low-rank projection, inflating the norm; at full contamination, the uniform synthetic signal reduces this conflict~\citep{dettmers2023qlora}.
This method-dependence means gradient norm cannot be used as a collapse indicator without knowing the training configuration (Figure~\ref{fig:signal_heatmap}).

\paragraph{Downstream and diversity metrics: insensitive at 0.5B.}
HellaSwag accuracy is insensitive under QLoRA (relative change $-1.15\%$; $N=1$ seed at 0.5B, no effect size computable).
Under full fine-tuning, the $\alpha = 0$ baseline is unavailable, preventing direct effect size computation; the available data show accuracy of $0.397$ ($\alpha = 0.5$) and $0.372$ ($\alpha = 1.0$), a $-6.3\%$ relative change between these two conditions.

Distinct-1 is non-monotonic under QLoRA: $+17.7\%$ at $\alpha = 0.5$ but $-12.5\%$ at $\alpha = 1.0$, reversing direction between moderate and full contamination.
Self-BLEU is insensitive to collapse even when evaluation perplexity increases $17\times$.
This disconnect arises because nucleus sampling ($p = 0.95$) draws from the distribution tail, producing superficially diverse surface forms even as the model's probability mass concentrates on fewer modes.
Token entropy captures this concentration (Section~\ref{sec:correlation}), but $n$-gram diversity metrics do not.
Monitoring pipelines that rely solely on output diversity metrics risk missing collapse entirely.

\paragraph{Full fine-tuning collapse dynamics.}
Full fine-tuning produces sharper onset but lower terminal severity than QLoRA (Figure~\ref{fig:method_comparison}).
The generation~0 to generation~1 evaluation perplexity ratio is $15.3\times$ under full FT versus $8.7\times$ under QLoRA.
Post-onset, the trajectory is non-monotonic: evaluation perplexity \emph{decreases} from $294.0$ at generation~1 to $288.5$ at generation~2 before rising through generations~3--4 to a terminal value of $326.19$.
This generation~2 dip echoes the partial recovery observed at moderate contamination (Section~\ref{sec:taxonomy}), suggesting that full parameter access allows transient re-adaptation even under full synthetic pressure.
The overall generation~1 to generation~4 ratio remains $1.11\times$, compared to continued monotonic growth under QLoRA, and terminal severity is lower: $\mathrm{PPL}_\text{eval} = 326.19$ versus QLoRA's $839.2$ ($0.39\times$).
This pattern---fast onset, partial dip, then resumed rise at lower terminal severity---is consistent with full parameter access enabling rapid adaptation to synthetic data characteristics.

We observe that terminal stable rank values are similar across methods: $\mathrm{SR} = 153.87$ (full FT) versus $155.64$ (QLoRA) at generation~4, $\alpha = 1.0$.
This comparison rests on $N = 1$ seed per method and cannot be distinguished from coincidence; we note it as an observation, not a finding.

\paragraph{Partial recovery at moderate contamination.}
At $\alpha = 0.5$, signals show partial recovery across generations relative to the $\alpha = 1.0$ trajectory.
Output signals (evaluation perplexity, token entropy) recover approximately 52\% of the clean-to-collapsed gap, while weight-space signals (stable rank, spectral entropy) recover approximately 33\%.
This pattern is consistent with data accumulation effects~\citep{Gerstgrasser2024}: the retained real data fraction attenuates collapse pressure.
Recovery ratios are computed within each signal family; cross-family prevalence comparisons are not meaningful because the signals have different scales and sensitivity profiles.

\paragraph{Recommended operating ranges.}
Based on the evidence above, we propose signal-to-task assignments (Table~\ref{tab:signal_taxonomy}):
\begin{itemize}[nosep]
    \item \textbf{Within-generation alarm:} stable rank ($\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.94$ at 10\% progress, $0.984$ pooled).
    \item \textbf{Cross-generation severity discrimination:} spectral entropy ($d = 33.48$, $\mathrm{CV} = 0.0015$).
    \item \textbf{Cross-generation tracking:} evaluation perplexity (large absolute effect, interpretable scale).
    \item \textbf{Method-dependent:} gradient norm (monotonic under full FT only).
    \item \textbf{Non-monotonic:} distinct-1 ($+17.7\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.5$, $-12.5\%$ at $\alpha{=}1.0$ under QLoRA).
    \item \textbf{Insensitive at 0.5B scale:} HellaSwag accuracy (relative change ${<}3\%$, $N{=}1$).
\end{itemize}

\noindent
Effect sizes in Section~\ref{sec:correlation} are from C2 (1.5B, $N=3$ interim seeds); within-generation AUROC values are from C1 (0.5B, $N=1$ seed); method-dependent operating ranges are from C1 vs C4 (0.5B, $N=1$ seed each).
Validation across larger models, additional domains, and larger seed counts is required before these operating ranges can be considered robust.

---

## Section 5: Discussion

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

\subsection{Practical Three-Tier Monitoring Recommendation}
\label{sec:three_tier}

No single signal suffices for collapse monitoring across all operating regimes.
Our results motivate a three-tier strategy that assigns each signal family to the task where it excels:

\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
    \item \textbf{Within-generation alarm} $\to$ stable rank.
    Stable rank achieves $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.94$ at 10\% training progress ($0.984$ pooled), with $\Delta_\mathrm{SR} = 34.4\%$ at step~50 (3\% of training).
    This structural sensitivity---detecting energy dispersal across representation dimensions before output-level metrics respond---provides the earliest actionable warning.

    \item \textbf{Cross-generation severity tracking} $\to$ evaluation perplexity.
    With a large absolute effect size ($d = 20.82$) and monotonic growth across generations, evaluation perplexity provides an interpretable severity scale that maps directly to language modeling quality on held-out text.

    \item \textbf{Severity discrimination} $\to$ spectral entropy.
    The largest effect size ($d = 33.48$) and lowest coefficient of variation ($\mathrm{CV} = 0.0015$) across seeds make spectral entropy the most reproducible discriminator between contamination levels.
\end{enumerate}

\noindent
This assignment reflects a core finding: the signal that best detects collapse onset (stable rank, $\mathrm{CV} = 0.022$, seed-sensitive) differs from the one that most reproducibly quantifies its severity (spectral entropy).

\subsection{Evaluation Perplexity: Within-Generation Failure Mechanism}
\label{sec:ppl_failure}

Evaluation perplexity achieves only overall $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.533$---indistinguishable from chance---despite being the primary severity indicator across generations.
As discussed in Section~\ref{sec:early_warning_results}, this failure is structural: collapse pressure enters only at the next generation, so evaluation perplexity accumulates degradation through the iterative loop, not within a single run.
Train loss ($\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.923$ at completion) is the second-strongest within-generation signal, but its trajectory reveals early-training direction reversal: AUROC starts at $0.24$ at 10\% progress (below chance) because the collapsing model's loss is initially \emph{lower}, recovering only as cumulative degradation raises loss in the second half of training (Section~\ref{sec:early_warning_results}).
For practitioners, the implication is that evaluation perplexity is a lagging indicator of collapse, and train loss changes require spectral cross-validation to interpret correctly.

\subsection{Partial Recovery at Moderate Contamination}
\label{sec:recovery}

At $\alpha = 0.5$, some signals show partial recovery across generations: output signals recover approximately 52\% of the clean-to-collapsed gap, while weight-space signals recover approximately 33\%.
This pattern is consistent with the data accumulation effects documented by \citet{Gerstgrasser2024}, where mixing real data with synthetic data attenuates collapse.
We note this as an observation, not a novel finding.
The practical consequence is that monitoring thresholds should be calibrated to the expected contamination level rather than set as binary collapsed/not-collapsed decisions.

\subsection{Comparison with Concurrent Monitoring Approaches}
\label{sec:sigma_comparison}

The signals evaluated here incur near-zero marginal cost: they are computed from quantities already available during standard training, require no clean reference distribution, and provide per-layer granularity.
SIGMA~\citep{Gu2026} operates post-hoc on the output embedding Gram matrix and requires a clean reference distribution for comparison.
\citet{Kalinowski2026} uses persistent homology, incurring higher computational cost from a different signal family entirely.
Neither provides the systematic comparison of signal families, operating range characterization across contamination fractions, or within-generation early warning documented here.
These approaches are complementary: SIGMA and topological methods may capture aspects of collapse that spectral covariance signals miss, while our signals offer the advantage of online, reference-free monitoring integrated into the training loop.

\subsection{Terminal Spectral Convergence}
\label{sec:terminal_convergence}

At generation~4, $\alpha = 1.0$, terminal stable rank values are $\mathrm{SR} = 153.87$ (full fine-tuning) versus $155.64$ (QLoRA)---a 1.2\% difference despite markedly different collapse dynamics (onset ratio $15.3\times$ vs $8.7\times$; terminal $\mathrm{PPL}_\text{eval}$ of $326.19$ vs $839.2$).
This observation rests on $N = 1$ seed per method and cannot be distinguished from coincidence.
If real, it would suggest that iterative synthetic contamination drives representations toward a method-independent attractor in spectral space---a convergence in representational structure despite divergent output-level severity.
Multi-seed validation is required before this can be treated as anything more than speculation.

---

## Section 6: Conclusion

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

We presented a systematic empirical study of training-time signals as model collapse severity monitors.
Across five experimental configurations spanning two model scales (0.5B--3B), two text domains (WikiText-2, PubMed), two fine-tuning methods (QLoRA, full fine-tuning), and six contamination fractions, we established three findings.

First, spectral and output signals reliably track collapse severity across configurations.
Spectral entropy achieves the largest and most reproducible effect size ($d = 33.48$, $\mathrm{CV} = 0.0015$ across seeds), followed by evaluation perplexity ($d = 20.82$) and stable rank ($d = 9.43$, $\mathrm{CV} = 0.022$).
Six of seven monitored signals maintain consistent direction of change regardless of training method.

Second, stable rank provides within-generation early warning, achieving $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.94$ at 10\% training progress ($0.984$ pooled) and 34.4\% deviation from baseline at 3\% of training.
Train loss provides the second-strongest within-generation signal (pooled $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.923$), though its decrease reflects successful fitting of corrupted data rather than improved model quality.
Held-out evaluation perplexity (pooled $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.533$) and token entropy (pooled $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.478$) fail at within-generation detection---the most commonly relied-upon quality metric is no better than chance at the most actionable task.

Third, signal informativeness depends on the fine-tuning method and model scale, motivating a three-tier monitoring strategy: stable rank for within-generation alarms, evaluation perplexity for cross-generation tracking, and spectral entropy for severity discrimination.

\paragraph{Future directions.}
Validating these findings at scales of practical interest ($\geq$7B) and across diverse domains would establish generalizability.
Translating early warning signals into automated intervention triggers---adaptive learning rate reduction, selective data filtering, or training rollback when spectral deviation exceeds calibrated thresholds---would close the loop from detection to mitigation.

---

## Limitations

Our study has several limitations that bound the scope of our conclusions.

\paragraph{Scale.}
Our primary experiments use Qwen2.5-0.5B and 1.5B models, with only a single-seed spot-check at 3B.
Whether signal--severity relationships and operating ranges transfer to models at scales of practical deployment ($\geq$7B) remains unvalidated.
Stable rank baselines are known to be scale-dependent~\citep{Jha2025}, and threshold calibration may require per-scale adjustment.

\paragraph{Seed count and statistical power.}
Cross-generation effect sizes are computed from $N = 3$ seeds (C2 configuration, interim 3 of 5 planned seeds); within-generation AUROC results use $N = 1$ seed at 0.5B (C1).
The full fine-tuning comparison (C4) uses $N = 1$ seed.
These sample sizes are insufficient for rank-based tests (minimum $p = 0.25$ for Wilcoxon with $N = 3$), and we rely on bootstrap confidence intervals.
Stable rank's coefficient of variation ($\mathrm{CV} = 0.022$) is an order of magnitude larger than spectral entropy's ($0.0015$), and its effect size dropped from $d = 61.7$ to $d = 9.43$ when a third seed was added---underscoring that our ranking of signals by sensitivity may shift with more seeds.

\paragraph{Domain coverage.}
We evaluate on WikiText-2 and PubMed abstracts.
Whether our signal taxonomy generalizes to code, dialogue, multilingual text, or instruction-following data is unknown.

\paragraph{Collapse source.}
Our iterative retraining protocol simulates a specific collapse mechanism---self-consuming loops with controlled contamination fractions.
Real-world collapse may involve mixed provenance (multiple model generations), distribution shift between generations, or partial synthetic contamination at unknown fractions.
Signal behavior under these conditions may differ from our controlled setting.

\paragraph{Fine-tuning methods.}
We compare QLoRA and full fine-tuning.
Other parameter-efficient methods (LoRA without quantization, adapters, prefix tuning) may interact differently with spectral signals due to different parameterization constraints.

\paragraph{Causal claims.}
We establish correlations between signals and collapse severity, not causal mechanisms.
The spectral entropy increase under collapse reflects a change in representation structure, but we do not prove that this change causes (rather than accompanies) output degradation.

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related_work}

\subsection{Model Collapse in Iterative Training}

The phenomenon of model collapse---progressive degradation when models are iteratively trained on their own outputs---has been established across multiple generative families.
\citet{Shumailov2024} provided the first systematic demonstration that iterative training on synthetic data causes distribution tails to vanish, leading to irreversible quality loss in LLMs, VAEs, and GMMs.
\citet{Alemohammad2024} formalized three self-consuming loop variants (fully synthetic, synthetic augmentation, and fresh data mixing), proving that without fresh real data, either precision or recall must degrade.
Theoretical analyses have since strengthened these findings: \citet{Dohmatob2025} proved via operator-valued free probability theory that even a $1/1000$ synthetic data fraction induces collapse and that larger models amplify the effect, while \citet{Dohmatob2024_tails} showed collapse alters scaling laws and induces systematic skill un-learning.
Further theoretical work has characterized error compounding across iterations~\citep{Fu2024_icml}, established safety thresholds for synthetic data fractions under statistical models~\citep{Seddik2024}, and revealed a generalization-to-memorization transition driven by data entropy~\citep{Shi2025_neurips}.
\citet{Schaeffer2025} catalogued eight distinct collapse definitions across three families, highlighting the need for precise operationalization.

Several lines of work study \emph{prevention} rather than detection.
\citet{Gerstgrasser2024} showed that data accumulation (rather than replacement) avoids collapse; \citet{Kazdan2024} systematically compared replacement, accumulation, and fixed-compute regimes; and verification-based approaches filter synthetic data to maintain quality~\citep{Feng2025,Yi2025}.
\citet{Gillman2024} demonstrated that correction functions can exponentially stabilize self-consuming loops, while \citet{Zibakhsh2025} proposed a truncated cross-entropy loss that increases tolerance to synthetic contamination by $2.3\times$.
\citet{Bakshi2026} (concurrent preprint) proved that even diminishing real data weights can prevent collapse in the long run.

These works collectively establish \emph{that} collapse occurs and \emph{how} to mitigate it, but they rely on post-hoc evaluation (test loss, distribution divergence) or require prior knowledge of contamination levels.
No prior work provides a real-time, training-time monitoring framework that tracks collapse severity as it develops.


\subsection{Training Dynamics as Diagnostic Signals}

\paragraph{Spectral analysis of neural networks.}
Spectral properties of weight matrices have emerged as powerful diagnostics for model quality and training health.
\citet{Martin2021} demonstrated that stable rank, spectral norm, and power-law exponents of weight spectra predict model quality without test data, establishing a random matrix theory (RMT) framework for neural network analysis.
\citet{Sanyal2020} proved a direct link between stable rank and generalization gap, showing that stable rank normalization improves generalization by up to 11.3\%.
More recently, \citet{Xu2026} (concurrent preprint) found stable rank to be the dominant predictor of LLM compression degradation (Pearson $r=0.890$) with informative per-layer variation between attention and MLP modules.
On the theoretical side, \citet{Pennington2017} extended RMT to nonlinear settings, deriving asymptotic spectral distributions through network layers.
\citet{Yunis2024} used spectral dynamics of weights to distinguish memorizing from generalizing networks, while \citet{AlphaPruning2024} validated per-layer spectral analysis for LLM quality assessment via alpha-exponent-guided pruning.

Spectral scaling across model sizes has received increasing attention.
\citet{Jha2025} discovered that FFN soft rank scales near-linearly with width while hard rank grows sub-linearly, implying that stable rank baselines are scale-dependent.
\citet{Staats2024} showed via RMT analysis across BERT, Pythia-410M, and Llama-8B that small singular values carry significant information, cautioning against truncated spectral analyses.
\citet{Liu2026_lifecycle} (concurrent preprint) documented the full spectral lifecycle of transformer training across three scales (30M--285M), revealing that stable rank compression propagates as a traveling wave from shallow to deep layers with Q/K and V/O asymmetries.

\paragraph{Training dynamics for data and training quality.}
Beyond weight spectra, training-time signals have been used to diagnose data quality and training health.
\citet{Li2025_gradient} showed that layer-wise gradient SVD effective rank and nuclear norm unify multiple data quality metrics, with higher effective rank indicating higher data quality.
\citet{Elgaar2026} (concurrent preprint) used gradient noise scale and singular entropy of the output head as LLM training diagnostics in curriculum learning.
\citet{Chen2024_dse} proposed diffusion spectral entropy (DSE) to track training dynamics, observing that information-theoretic measures stagnate at overfitting onset.
\citet{Qiu2025} introduced spectral alignment between layer inputs and weight principal singular vectors as an early predictor of loss explosion, detecting pathologies before gradient norms diverge.
\citet{Kalra2026} (concurrent preprint) proposed critical sharpness as a lightweight loss landscape curvature measure validated at 7B scale.

\paragraph{Closest competitors.}
Two concurrent works most directly relate to ours.
\textbf{SIGMA}~\citep{Gu2026} (concurrent preprint) analyzes the Gram matrix spectrum of output embeddings to quantify collapse, deriving spectral contraction bounds.
However, SIGMA operates as a post-hoc, black-box diagnostic: it requires a clean reference distribution, does not perform per-layer analysis, does not track within-generation training dynamics, and has not been validated in the iterative synthetic data setting.
\textbf{Kalinowski}~\citep{Kalinowski2026} (concurrent preprint) proposes an online topological monitor based on persistent homology with sparse incremental updates.
While this shares our goal of real-time monitoring, it uses a fundamentally different signal family (topological rather than spectral/entropic), incurs higher computational cost, and has not been evaluated on iterative synthetic data collapse.
Table~\ref{tab:competitor_comparison} summarizes the key differences.

Neither approach provides a systematic comparison of multiple signal families, documents where signals saturate or mislead, or establishes quantitative early warning thresholds for iterative collapse.


\subsection{Data Quality and Contamination Detection}

A parallel line of work addresses detection of synthetic data in training corpora.
Watermarking approaches embed identifiable patterns in generated text: \citet{Kirchenbauer2023} introduced green/red token list watermarking with statistical detection, while \citet{Dathathri2024} scaled watermarking to production (SynthID-Text, validated on ${\sim}$20M Gemini responses) and \citet{Sander2024} showed that watermark residuals can detect whether a model was trained on watermarked synthetic data.
Statistical detection methods identify machine-generated text without explicit watermarks: \citet{Mitchell2023} exploited log-probability curvature for zero-shot detection (DetectGPT), and \citet{Shi2024_mink} proposed Min-K\% Prob for membership inference in pretraining data.
At the dataset level, \citet{Penedo2024} documented quality filtering strategies for 15T-token web corpora, and \citet{Zhang2026} (concurrent preprint) proposed a unified quality-trustworthiness evaluation taxonomy for synthetic data.
\citet{Gambetta2024} introduced surplexity to quantify diversity loss from synthetic contamination at various mixture fractions, providing an output-level post-hoc analysis.
